A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on SSM–Transformer comparability. Their text, equations, figures and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial changes in title, architecture and scope.

before.justification: Section 6, Figure 6.1 and Appendix I report original HyenaDNA fine-tuning and token-masking results for classification and next-token prediction.

after.justification: Section 5 retains the classification experiment. Figure 1.1 and Appendix C additionally report trained-model heatmaps and synthetic-task comparisons.

M1.justification: The analyzed convolution changes from the explicitly gated operation (WQ X) multiplied elementwise by H*(WV X) in v1 Section 3 to H*(WX) alternating with FNNs in v2 Section 2. V2 also introduces a linear decoding layer and autoregressive output procedure for synthetic tasks. These change the model and inference construction.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual evaluations of input copying, associative recall and synthetic nonparametric regression. It retains human_enhancers_cohn classification but removes the demo_human_or_worm next-token experiment. Appendix D's additional tasks are theoretical, and Appendix E's ImageNet examples are illustrations rather than evaluated benchmarks.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates HyenaDNA without competing model baselines. V2 adds single- versus two-layer SSM comparisons with FNN depths 2 and 4, a Transformer accuracy baseline for input copying in Figure C.1, and SSM–Transformer heatmap comparisons in Figure 1.1. The recall and regression curves do not display Transformer baselines.

E3.justification: New synthetic protocols vary SSM layer count, FNN depth and state/model dimensions, reporting copying/recall accuracy and regression loss. Appendix C also specifies a regression target based on the maximum token-associated value. The retained DNA classification recipe remains 100 fine-tuning epochs and 20 selected high-confidence test sequences.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds controlled layer-count, FNN-depth and dimension sweeps examining when nonlinear layers help SSMs. Figure 1.1 adds token-importance case studies. The classification masking analysis remains, while v1's analysis of importance changing across output-token positions is removed.

E5.justification: The retained DNA experiment still reports standard deviations across 20 selected test sequences, not repeated training runs. V2 introduces no new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedure; the added synthetic curves have no reported uncertainty.

E6.justification: Figures C.1–C.2 add accuracy and loss curves showing advantages of two-layer SSMs with sufficiently expressive FNNs at smaller dimensions, including copying performance approaching the Transformer baseline. Figure 1.1 adds empirical token-importance findings. The classification masking finding is retained, while Figure 6.1's next-token results disappear.

T1.justification: V2 adds explicit copying, recall, induction-head and selective-copying theorems, formalizes token selection in Lemma 3.3, and derives finite-window reproduction. Regression changes to scalar output and gamma-smooth importance functions; the gamma-smooth approximation theorem moves to Appendix I.1, while its standalone estimation theorem and separate similarity-based regression case disappear. The piecewise-risk bound changes from log^10 V to log^13 V, with revised log n exponents. New Lemma F.6 also leaves its N-term statement unreconciled with its N^d-term proof construction.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds statistical estimation of smoothness-structured functions and an extension allowing output-position-dependent importance. V2 foregrounds efficient synthetic-task solutions and the ability of SSMs surrounded by FNNs to emulate dynamic token selection, with regression as another application. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion substantially redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new comparisons as evidence that FNNs before and after an SSM enable dynamic selection, extending v1's gated-kernel explanation. It adds substantive qualifications about block-diagonal versus customary diagonal state matrices and explains selective-copying vocabulary restrictions through overlapping token patterns. The optimization and unstudied-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix K retains the classification experiment's software, A100 hardware, access links, model, training duration and scripts. It removes the next-token model, scripts and resource details previously documented in Appendix I. Added synthetic experiments identify architectural configurations and dimension grids but provide little corresponding training or reproducibility detail.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from a gap in statistical comparison toward overcoming limitations attributed to single SSM layers through nonlinear layers. V2 introduces a central comparison with Jelassi et al. on copying and quantifies its claimed recall advantage over Massaroli et al. New citations also support embedding constructions, induction heads and illustrative applications.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around dynamic token selection. Model definitions now precede synthetic tasks and regression; approximation and estimation material is reorganized, with gamma-smooth approximation moved into the appendix. Appendix E adds substantial intuitive explanation of the function classes.

P2.justification: Figure 1.1 is redesigned from illustrative token sequences into a mechanism comparison with empirical heatmaps. The classification panel of Figure 6.1 becomes the smaller, text-wrapped Figure 5.1, while the next-token panel is removed. Figures C.1–C.2 and E.1–E.2 add performance plots, explanatory diagrams and application illustrations.

improvement.justification: V2 improves mechanism exposition and adds directly relevant model comparisons absent from v1. However, its new efficiency guarantees rely on Lemma F.6, whose N-term claim is not reconciled with the N^d-term construction in its proof. This unresolved central support, alongside limited training and uncertainty documentation for the added experiments, prevents a reliable net quality judgment despite the clearer presentation and broader evidence.
